tldr: We propose a robot manipulation framework that incorporates execution-time tactile feedback without separate high-frequency controllers, achieved through streaming action generation in blocks and an attention design that restricts conditioning to the most recent tactile information.
hero_caption: Overall framework of TacForcing. Global vision and language task context is encoded once at the beginning and reused, while action blocks are generated and executed sequentially. Newly acquired tactile feedback obtained immediately after execution is routed to refine the next block scheduled for execution.
overview:
In contact-rich manipulation tasks where a robot interacts with objects, adapting immediately to evolving contact states—such as applied forces and slips—is essential. Modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models predominantly predict actions in chunks, but this comes with a major catch: relying solely on tactile observations collected before chunk execution leaves tactile conditioning stale as contact states change rapidly during execution. Conversely, introducing a separate low-level reactive controller for high-frequency tactile adaptation significantly complicates both system architecture and training pipelines.

To address this, the authors introduce "TacForcing," which combines sequential action execution and tactile updates within a single action-generation model. An action chunk is partitioned into multiple blocks; the earliest block is finished first and dispatched for execution, while unfinished blocks maintain their intermediate generation states. As soon as a block completes execution, the model resumes generation from these preserved states using freshly acquired tactile feedback. Furthermore, because exposing distant future actions to the newest tactile data causes temporal misalignment, the authors introduce Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), which restricts tactile conditioning exclusively to the next block scheduled for execution.

Evaluated on six simulation tasks and three real-world multi-fingered hand manipulation tasks, TacForcing achieves an average success rate of 65% in simulation and 69% in the real world. It substantially outperforms tactile-free and fixed-tactile baselines, as well as hierarchical tactile-reactive methods, demonstrating strong contact adaptation capabilities.
contributions: Proposed "TacForcing," a streaming action generation framework that incorporates execution-time tactile feedback within a single model without requiring a separate reactive controller.
Developed a Flow Scheduling method that generates and executes action chunks progressively by blocks, refining downstream actions with fresh tactile feedback while preserving intermediate states.

Introduced Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), an attention mechanism that restricts direct access to fresh tactile updates to the immediately scheduled action block, mitigating temporal misalignment between sensing and execution.

Demonstrated significant success rate improvements across six simulation tasks and three real-world tasks over strong baselines, including vision-only, fixed-tactile, and separate reactive controller approaches.

sections.heading: Why is integrating tactile feedback into VLAs so challenging?
sections.summary: Existing chunk-based VLA models cannot keep up with rapid contact changes during execution, while relying on separate high-speed controllers makes system design complicated. This paper proposes "TacForcing," a streaming action generation framework that integrates execution-time tactile feedback while preserving intermediate generation states.
sections.details:
Contact-rich tasks, such as precision assembly and peg insertion, demand not only semantic task understanding but also continuous adaptation to dynamic contact states. While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at semantic generalization, visual inputs alone cannot accurately capture applied forces, slippage, or contacts hidden under occlusions.

Efforts to incorporate tactile feedback face a critical obstacle: temporal mismatch. While visual features remain largely unchanged over a one-second window, tactile signals can fluctuate drastically within a single executed action chunk. If an entire chunk is predicted based purely on initial tactile readings, the discrepancy between the later actions and real-world contact conditions compounds rapidly. Prior tactile-reactive approaches typically combine a slow visual policy with a separate high-frequency controller, but this introduces considerable architectural and training complexity.

TacForcing solves this dilemma. It divides an action chunk into blocks, prioritizing the generation and execution of the nearest block while keeping subsequent blocks in an intermediate generative state to be refined by fresh tactile feedback. Paired with Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), which channels new tactile information strictly to the immediately upcoming block, TacForcing achieves high tactile reactivity without needing an auxiliary controller.

captions.F1: TacForcing processing pipeline. The VLM encodes visual and language observations once into a global task context, and the Streaming Action Expert generates action blocks with staggered schedules. Fingertip tactile feedback updates after each block executes and is incorporated into the generation of the next block.

sections.heading: Rapid tactile drift and the pitfall of "fixed tactile" conditioning
sections.summary: We review the formulation of Flow Matching for action generation and experimentally demonstrate the stark contrast between vision and tactile dynamics during dropper manipulation. While visual features remain virtually static during chunk execution, tactile features drift significantly, explaining why conditioning on initial tactile observations causes failures.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Preliminaries: Flow Matching
The framework uses Flow Matching (FM) as its generative backbone, learning a continuous vector field that maps a noise distribution to a data distribution. Under conditioning $y$, a noise sample $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and a data sample $x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot \mid y)$ are linearly interpolated, and the velocity field $v_\theta$ is trained by minimizing mean squared error. At inference time, actions are sampled by integrating the learned velocity field from time $\tau=0$ to $\tau=1$.

### 2.2 Problem Formulation and Standard Action Generation Constraints
The robot receives task context $c_t$ (composed of visual observations $V_t$, proprioceptive state $s_t$, and language instruction $\ell$) along with tactile observation $T_t$, predicting an action chunk $A_t = [a_t, \ldots, a_{t+H-1}]$ over horizon $H$. However, standard flow-based action experts share a single flow time across all action steps, generating the entire chunk in one shot conditioned on fixed initial observations $(c_t, T_t)$. Consequently, tactile feedback collected mid-execution cannot inform subsequent actions within the same chunk.

### 2.3 Empirical Evidence of Tactile Drift
The authors measured feature drift using cosine distance during a dropper squeezing and liquid suction task (40 steps, $\approx 1.17$ seconds). Compared to the initial observation, visual features drifted by only 0.005, whereas tactile features at the thumb and index finger drifted by 0.55. In other words, while the robot's eyes perceive a nearly static scene, the physical sensation on its fingertips changes drastically. This dramatic divergence is the core reason why policies conditioned on static, chunk-initial tactile observations struggle in contact-rich manipulation.

(b) Fingertip deformation map trajectories for thumb and index finger. (c) Cosine distance from the initial features. Tactile features drift considerably ($\approx 0.55$) compared to visual features ($\approx 0.005$).

sections.heading: Block-wise flow scheduling and EATA
sections.summary: We introduce an interleaved execution-and-generation mechanism by partitioning action chunks into blocks with staggered flow times. Furthermore, an attention mask (EATA) routes newly acquired tactile feedback exclusively to the upcoming execution block, preventing inappropriate tactile leakage into distant future actions.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Streaming Generation via Block-Wise Flow Scheduling
Running full diffusion/flow inference at every single control step is computationally prohibitive. TacForcing instead divides the action horizon $H$ into $K$ contiguous blocks of size $B$ ($H=KB$). Across $N=KS$ total sampling steps, each block $k$ is assigned a staggered completion step $n_k = kS$. The earliest block $A_t^{(1)}$ finishes generation first and is immediately dispatched to the robot, while future blocks pause at intermediate states. Staggering execution and generation in this manner minimizes inference latency while creating natural entry points for execution-time feedback.

### 3.2 Execution-Time Tactile Feedback and Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA)
The global vision-language context $C_t$ is encoded once per chunk and reused. In contrast, tactile observations $T_t^{(k)}$ are updated whenever block $k$ finishes execution by passing fingertip deformation maps through an encoder to produce tactile tokens $Z_t^{(k)}$.
Here, the design of EATA is critical. Fresh tactile feedback $Z_t^{(k-1)}$ collected right after block execution is timely for the immediately upcoming block $A_t^{(k)}$, but represents premature conditioning for blocks scheduled further down the line. If all blocks attend to this feedback unconditionally, distant future actions will be biased toward early tactile states. To prevent this, TacForcing employs an attention mask $\mathcal{M}^{(k)}$ that allows only queries from the next execution block $A_t^{(k)}$ to attend to the latest tactile tokens, withholding tactile access from subsequent blocks until their turn for execution arrives.

### 3.3 Training Procedure
To match streaming inference conditions during training, a progress scalar $p \sim \mathcal{U}([0, 1))$ is randomly sampled. Based on $p$, intermediate states and flow times are determined for each block. Flow matching velocity loss is then computed exclusively on action tokens of currently unfinished blocks, using their corresponding execution-stage tactile tokens and the EATA mask.

sections.heading: Contact-rich manipulation benchmarks in simulation and real-world
sections.summary: TacForcing was evaluated against vision-only, fixed-tactile, and separate-controller baselines across six simulation and three real-world tasks. It achieved top performance with a 65% success rate in simulation and 69% in the real world, with ablations confirming that both execution-time updates and EATA are indispensable.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
- Benchmarks: Six tasks in the UniVTAC simulation environment (Bottle Pick, Key Pull, Can Pick, Shelf Place, Slot Insertion, Tube Insertion) and three real-world tasks (Stand Bottle, Transfer Liquid, Wipe Board).
- Baselines: Tactile-free $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7, pretrained tactile-conditioned UniVTAC-ACT and FTP-1, and RDP, which pairs a policy with a high-frequency reactive controller.
- Implementation: Block size $B=5$. Simulation uses $H=50$ ($K=10$ blocks), and real-world experiments use $H=40$ ($K=8$ blocks). Evaluation comprises 100 trials per task in simulation and 16 trials per task on the real robot.

### 4.2 Main Results
- Simulation Results: TacForcing achieved an average success rate of 65%, outperforming vision-only $\pi_{0.5}$ (51%) by 14 percentage points and the hierarchical reactive RDP (42%) by 23 percentage points. It achieved the best or tied-best performance in five out of six tasks.
- Real-World Results: TacForcing achieved an average success rate of 69%, substantially outperforming strong baselines such as FTP-1 (52%), GR00T N1.7 (42%), and $\pi_{0.5}$ (27%). In "Transfer Liquid," which demands delicate force regulation, baseline success rates peaked at 19%, whereas TacForcing reached 50%.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies
To isolate the impact of individual design components, four configurations were evaluated:
1. Base (no tactile): 43% sim / 42% real
2. Fixed Tactile (static chunk-initial tactile): 42% sim / 31% real (fixed tactile can actually degrade real-world performance)
3. TacForcing without EATA (streaming updates without attention masking): 51% sim / 48% real
4. TacForcing (full proposed method): 60% sim / 69% real
While execution-time updates alone provide notable gains, incorporating EATA to isolate tactile attention to the upcoming block produced an additional 21-percentage-point jump on the real robot (from 48% to 69%), highlighting the necessity of temporally aligned tactile conditioning.

captions.F3: Real-world setup and task evaluation results. (a) Snapshots of "Stand Bottle," "Transfer Liquid," and "Wipe Board." (b) Success rate comparison against baselines. TacForcing achieves 50% on Transfer Liquid, far outperforming the best baseline at 19%.

sections.heading: Streaming diffusion models and the tactile robotics landscape
sections.summary: We review streaming generation techniques such as Diffusion Forcing alongside prior tactile policy research for contact-rich manipulation. TacForcing bridges these fields, enabling single-model execution-time tactile adaptation without separate low-level controllers or explicit contact forecasting.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Diffusion and Flow Models for Sequence Generation
While Flow Matching and diffusion models are widely adopted for trajectory generation, they standardly assign a uniform generation step across the full horizon and wait for generation to conclude before execution begins. To mitigate latency, frameworks like Diffusion Forcing assign token-specific noise schedules, and rolling-buffer techniques have been explored in robotics. However, these methods primarily address inference latency rather than the temporal alignment of rapidly changing physical feedback within an execution chunk. TacForcing adapts this streaming paradigm to solve execution-time tactile integration.

### 5.2 Tactile Policies for Contact-Rich Manipulation
Prior robotics literature has explored tactile-visual representation learning and multimodal VLA pretraining. However, these approaches largely bypass the temporal challenge of conditioning ongoing action horizons on streaming sensor streams. Prior execution-time adaptation frameworks typically rely either on decoupling a slow visual policy from a fast reactive controller or on forecasting future contact states explicitly. TacForcing stands apart by resolving this challenge end-to-end within a single streaming action model without auxiliary controllers or explicit contact predictors.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: TacForcing combines streaming action generation with EATA to enable execution-time tactile adaptation without auxiliary controllers. Delivering strong empirical improvements in simulation and real-world experiments, it underscores the importance of temporally synchronizing tactile feedback with action execution.
sections.details:
This paper presented TacForcing, a novel streaming action-generation framework designed to adapt to rapid contact state variations during action chunk execution.

By leveraging a Streaming Action Expert, the system sequentially generates and executes action blocks, holding unfinished blocks in intermediate states and refining them with incoming execution-time tactile feedback. Furthermore, Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA) restricts fresh tactile observations to the next execution block, eliminating temporal mismatch. Achieving high average success rates of 65% across six simulation tasks and 69% across three real-world tasks, the framework's effectiveness is thoroughly validated by ablation experiments. The findings establish that in contact-rich robotics, simply providing tactile observations is not enough—synchronizing feedback with the exact execution timeline is crucial.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-world bimanual setup and task details
sections.summary: The real-world system uses two 7-DoF arms and two 22-DoF dexterous hands with tactile fingertips, teleoperated via data gloves. Detailed task requirements and training hyperparameters for both simulation and real-world experiments are provided.
sections.details:
### Real-World Hardware Platform
The real-world robot setup consists of two 7-DoF manipulator arms (RealMan RM75) and two 22-DoF dexterous hands (Sharpa Wave) equipped with fingertip tactile sensors that output contact deformation maps. Visual sensing relies on a top camera (RealSense) capturing the workspace alongside two wrist cameras mounted on each arm. Teleoperated demonstration data was recorded using Manus Pro data gloves.

### Task Specifications and Training Hyperparameters
- Real-World Tasks:
  - Stand Bottle: Grasp a horizontal bottle, perform an in-hand reorientation in mid-air, and place it upright without toppling.
  - Transfer Liquid: Grasp and operate a dropper under visual occlusion to draw liquid from a flask and transfer it into a beaker.
  - Wipe Board: Press an eraser firmly against a whiteboard with regulated force and sweep across marker strokes to erase them.
- Training Parameters:
  - Real-world training uses 100 demonstrations per task, optimized with AdamW (peak learning rate $6 \times 10^{-5}$) at batch size 256 for 30,000 steps.
  - Simulation training uses 50 demonstrations per task from UniVTAC for 15,000 steps.
  - The block size is consistently set to $B=5$ actions.

takeaways: In chunk-based action prediction, reusing the initial tactile reading across all steps fails to follow contact dynamics and can even harm performance.
Without adding a separate high-frequency controller, staggering generation flow times across blocks in a single Flow model allows seamless execution-time feedback integration.
Restricting fresh sensor feedback to the immediately upcoming action block via targeted attention (EATA), rather than broadcasting it globally, is critical for avoiding temporal mismatch.
limitations: The block size ($B=5$) and sampling step allocation are fixed, lacking a mechanism to dynamically adapt update frequencies to fast-changing task dynamics.
Global vision-language context from the VLM is encoded once at chunk initiation and kept static, leaving the system unequipped to adapt to sudden visual shifts or occlusion clearing mid-chunk.
Collecting demonstrations on the real-world setup requires specialized, expensive data gloves compatible with dexterous hands, posing higher adoption barriers than standard parallel grippers.
